(e) Only routed items are affected, so under the keyword router about a third of the dev panel is diluted by E1's leak. Either force routing for E2 or run it after E1. The falsifier for invented person facts is sound, but it only sees what the G2 regex misses. Novelty is thinner than stated. DIVERGE (2602.00238, abstract-only) already conditions each generation on a different retrieved viewpoint with diversity-aware MMR, and reports that simply diversifying retrieval does not make generations diverse. Memory-assisted personalised recommenders (e.g. MAP 2505.03824, abstract-only) retrieve personal-memory facts to condition generation. What stays new is a hard no-invention guard at 1B on an exact triple store, which counts as novel only in the suggested sense.

E3 (sleep DivPO/DDPO) is the weakest. The DDPO evidence depends on human-written, many-per-prompt data. Self-samples from a low-variety 1B give little deviation to weight. The quality label has to come from an LLM judge, which risks training toward the grader (the report notes this but builds nothing to stop it). The 150-per-1000 target is arbitrary, and its baseline (45-59) was measured on the old generative mouth, not the 333d path, so the comparison is not like for like. The weights are shared by every path, so 'within 1 item' on two suites is too narrow a regression check. The whole e2e suite should be re-run. A 10-item human check cannot falsify anything. Before E3, the NoveltyBench 1B result suggests checking whether the pipeline, not the weights, causes the low variety.

Across all three, the pass marks are fixed in advance and each names a falsifier, which is good. None controls for LLM-judge variance: two judge passes or a second judge model would fix that.
verdict.missed: 1. SHOWN from code: the 333d creative path sends the model only [system prompt + notebook facts, current user message]. No chat history reaches it, while the plain twin that scored 10/40 saw the whole chat. Anything taught in chat prose but not stored as a triple, plus the request's conversational context, is lost on the creative path. The cleanest single-change experiment the report missed is to give the creative path the recent chat turns (or the twin's context) with the guards unchanged. It is a brain-like episodic-context change and cheaper than E2. 2. SHOWN: the report never asks whether the creative path beats the ordinary reply at all. An oracle-routing comparison should come before E1. 3. Personalisation-induced hallucination: 'When Personalization Misleads' (2601.11000, FPPS/PFQABench). It is the direct ML counterpart of the schema-distortion story, with an inference-time steering fix. The report's author downloaded it into the shared scratch dir but did not cite it. 4. Diversity-with-quality training that the report missed: DARLING (2509.02534, abstract-only: a learned semantic-equivalence classifier combined with quality in online RL) and Creative Preference Optimization (2505.14442, not opened). Both are closer to a sleep-phase recipe than DDPO. 5. DIVERGE (2602.00238, abstract-only) as prior art for per-sample cue retrieval, and its warning that diverse retrieval does not by itself give diverse outputs. 6. From the cited Dreaming paper: the symbolic structured-replay arm was the robust positive, and in-context remote material hurt. 7. NoveltyBench's finding that 1B models are among the most diverse, which points the variety failure at the pipeline. 8. Small effect sizes in Chen 2025, and that its task study found no link between switching frequency and originality. Plain-language note for Ben: the report cites its sources mostly correctly, but some are better news for big models than for yours. The simplest thing it missed is that your creative path currently can't see the conversation, only the saved facts. Try giving it the chat before trying anything fancier.

report.angle: How to choose the best of several candidate replies, and how to measure creativity: small learned reward models, LLM judges and their length and flattery biases, creative-writing benchmarks and diversity metrics, and how to reward the correct use of taught facts without rewarding invented ones.
report.summary: I read 17 primary sources: 16 arXiv papers, most from 2023-2026, plus Li et al. 2016 on dialogue. Six results bear most directly on Premonition. (1) Small learned reward models trained on preference data beat zero-shot judges on creative writing. LitBench (2507.00769) reports 78% agreement with humans for trained models, 73% for the best frontier judge and 56-60% for small open judges. Asking the reward model to reason first made it worse (72%). (2) Length bias is the main trap. It lives mostly in the reward model (2310.03716), and a Llama-3.2-1B reward model trained on data that was not length-filtered "strongly preferred the longer story" (2507.00769). A small regression that controls for length fixes much of it in judges (2404.04475). (3) Skywork-Reward-V2 ships ready-made 0.6B and Llama-3.2-1B reward models (2507.01352). On an independent personalization benchmark the 1B one scores within a few points of frontier judges (2604.07343), but it is weak on 'ties' and factuality at 0.6B. (4) Pickers based on plain likelihood choose generic, safe non-answers. That was known in 2016 (1510.03055), which proposed a mutual-information reranker. Context-aware decoding (2305.14739) uses the same with-context versus without-context contrast to reduce hallucination. Together these suggest a picker that rewards replies which depend on the notebook, not replies that merely match it. (5) Measuring creativity: LLM judges did not correlate with expert creativity ratings on the TTCW tests (2309.14556). Query-specific rubrics raise agreement with humans to 79-87% versus 40-69% for fixed rubrics (2503.05244). Diversity should be reported as compression ratio + Self-BLEU + long-n-gram repetition, because type/token-ratio scores mostly track length (2403.00553). NoveltyBench's distinct_k/utility_k counts useful and distinct outputs together, and Llama-3.2-1B was very diverse but low in utility (2504.05228). (6) From the code (scripts/claude_cre333d_agent.py): 333d has no real picker. It returns the first of 4 samples that passes the guards, and the creative path sends only the system prompt, the notebook facts and the current message, never the earlier chat. The twin got the whole chat. That is a confound in the 8/40 vs 10/40 comparison, and I did not test it. Plain version for Ben: the old picker chose the safest, shortest answer, the way a nervous student writes one careful sentence. The research says to train a small judge on examples of human preferences, keep it from rewarding length, and separately reward replies that actually use what you taught the assistant. Note that 40 requests is a small panel: 8 vs 10 useful is within noise, so the pass marks below require bigger gaps.

findings.claim: Bradley-Terry and generative reward models fine-tuned on 43.8k human creative-writing preference pairs reach 78% agreement with humans on a debiased test set. The best zero-shot judge (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) reaches 73%, and smaller open-source zero-shot judges reach 56-60%.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: A small trained preference model is a more reliable creative picker than asking a small LLM to judge. It also supports the owner's preference for learned parts over rules.

findings.claim: Adding chain-of-thought to generative reward models lowered creative-writing verdict accuracy from about 78% to 72%. Without chain-of-thought, generative reward models did not improve significantly from 1B/1.5B up to larger backbones.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Any MiniCPM5-1B self-judge should run with enable_thinking=False. That fits the 333 finding that leaving thinking on broke the creative path.

findings.claim: A Llama-3.2-1B Bradley-Terry reward model trained on creative pairs that were not length-filtered was length-biased and 'strongly preferred the longer of the two stories in most cases'. Balancing the length differences in the training pairs removed this.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: If Premonition trains its own picker during sleep, the replayed preference pairs must be length-balanced, or the picker becomes a length detector.

findings.claim: In RLHF, most of the reward gain comes from longer responses, and a reward based purely on length reproduces most of the downstream RLHF improvements. The main source of the bias is the reward model.
findings.source: arXiv 2310.03716 (Singhal et al., COLM 2024), abstract and Fig. 1
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Picking with any off-the-shelf reward model should be checked by asking whether it just picks the longest candidate.

findings.claim: Regressing judge preferences on length difference and predicting at zero difference (length-controlled AlpacaEval) cut verbosity-prompt gameability: the baseline's win rate range shrank from 22.9-64.3% to 41.9-51.6%. Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena rose from 0.94 to 0.98.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: The blind 40-item creative judge can report a length-controlled preference at almost no cost. The 23/40 'preferred or tied' may partly reflect length.

findings.claim: Across 12 injected judge biases, position bias gets worse as more candidates are shown at once: with 3-4 options, robustness falls below 0.5 for most judges. Biases are larger on alignment/open-ended data than on fact data, because quality gaps there are smaller. Sentiment robustness was only 0.65-0.80.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Creative requests are exactly the small-gap setting where judges are most biased. Judge in pairs with the order swapped, never 4-way. A warm or flattering tone may be rewarded regardless of usefulness.

findings.claim: Both humans and preference models prefer convincingly written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time, and optimizing against preference models sometimes trades truthfulness for sycophancy.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: A reward-model picker may favor warm replies that confirm the user's premises, including invented details about their people. The invented-person guard must stay a hard filter, not a score term.

findings.claim: Skywork-Reward-V2 includes 0.6B (Qwen3) and 1B (Llama-3.2) reward models. On RM-Bench style-bias splits the 0.6B scores 90.3/78.0/54.8 (easy/normal/hard) and the 1B 91.3/79.9/57.8. On RewardBench v2 the 0.6B is weak on Factuality (58.2) and Ties (34.0).
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: A ready-made reward model that fits on the 5090 next to MiniCPM5-1B. Its weak factuality means it cannot be trusted to catch invented facts, so the notebook guard must remain.

findings.claim: On Personalized RewardBench (pairs that differ only in whether they follow a user-specific rubric), Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2-1B scores 62.1/70.8/67.9% across three domains. Claude-Sonnet-4-6 scores 67.3/70.7/73.6% and the best model (Gemini-3-Flash) at most 75.9%.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: On this benchmark, a 1B scalar reward model is about as good as frontier judges at telling which reply fits a particular user. It is a plausible picker for replies that use taught facts.

findings.claim: LLMs used as personalized judges (judging preferences from a persona) show low and inconsistent agreement with humans. Letting the judge state its uncertainty and keeping only high-certainty verdicts gives more than 80% agreement on binary tasks.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Judging 'did this reply use my facts well' is itself unreliable. Report abstentions or low-confidence items separately in the creative judge.

findings.claim: Personalization can cause 'personalization-induced hallucination': the model answers in line with the user's history instead of the truth.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Rewarding fact use too strongly may push the 1B model to bend the request toward notebook facts, or to confabulate around them.

findings.claim: Ranking by likelihood of the response given the message selects generic safe replies such as 'I don't know'. Reranking the N-best list with the mutual-information term log p(S|T), with a tuned length weight, gave more specific replies that human judges preferred (alpha = 0.05).
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: This is the 333 failure (the picker preferred short grounded non-answers), and it has a known fix: score how much the reply depends on the input, not how safe it is.

findings.claim: Context-aware decoding, which contrasts output probabilities with and without the context, improved faithfulness to the context without training (for example +14.3% on factuality metrics for LLaMA in summarization). It helps most when the context conflicts with the model's prior knowledge.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: The same with-notebook versus without-notebook contrast, computed by MiniCPM5-1B itself, could score whether a candidate actually depends on taught facts. Using it as a picker score, rather than for decoding, is my untested extension.

findings.claim: LLM assessors administering the 14 TTCW tests did not correlate positively with 10 expert creative writers: average correlations were close to zero, and GPT-4 exceeded 0.2 on only 2 of the 14 tests.
findings.source: arXiv 2309.14556 (Chakrabarty et al., CHI 2024), Sec. 6 and Table 9
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Torrance-style originality scores from an LLM judge are not trustworthy. Premonition's 'useful' judgement is a more tractable target than 'creative'.

findings.claim: Query-specific rubrics (5 criteria generated per request) reached 79% (GPT-4o) and 87% (Claude-3.7) human consistency, versus 40-69% for fixed global or domain rubrics. A Qwen-2.5-7B critic fine-tuned on 155k scored examples reached 84%.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: The 40-item creative judge would likely be more reliable if each request carried its own 'what would make this useful' criteria, fixed before any replies are generated.

findings.claim: Type/token-ratio diversity scores are highly correlated with text length. Self-BLEU has low length correlation. The authors recommend reporting compression ratio, POS compression, Self-BLEU and self-repetition of long n-grams.
findings.source: arXiv 2403.00553 (Shaib et al.), Sec. 5 and abstract
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: The variety metric (45-59 distinct replies per 1000) and any distinct-n measure should be length-matched or replaced by compression ratio + Self-BLEU.

findings.claim: NoveltyBench measures distinct_k (functional-equivalence classes among k samples, from a DeBERTa classifier with 79% accuracy against humans) and utility_k, a reward-model quality score that counts only novel generations and is discounted by user patience p=0.8. Llama-3.2-1B had high distinctness (6.74/10) but low utility (2.81). Asking for 'unique' outputs in the system prompt helped only marginally, while in-context regeneration helped more.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: A ready-made way to score variety and usefulness together. It suggests a 1B model has plenty of diversity to draw on, and what it lacks is a picker that keeps the useful variants.

findings.claim: Weighting DPO/ORPO pairs by the winner's deviation from other samples for the same prompt raised output diversity with a minimal quality loss. An 8B model matched the diversity of a human-written dataset at quality similar to GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1.
findings.source: arXiv 2503.17126 (Chung et al.), abstract and Sec. 3
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: A candidate recipe for the sleep phase: replay chosen/rejected creative pairs weighted by rarity. It would fit the brain analogy, but it needs training, which is beyond this month.

findings.claim: CrPO injects novelty, diversity, surprise and quality signals into preference optimization and reports gains over GPT-4o on automated and human evaluations. The paper also notes a trade-off in which some creativity injections lower quality.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: A multi-signal creative reward is feasible, but mixing signals trades off quality. Prefer changing one signal at a time.

findings.claim: Self-certainty (KL divergence of the token distribution from uniform) works as a best-of-N selector without a reward model and stays largely invariant to response length. Its 'open-ended' results cover math and code, not creative text.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: This is a cheap picker, but it rewards confident, typical text. Applied to creative replies it would probably reproduce the generic-safe-reply failure, which is why I rank it below the reward-model and mutual-information pickers.

findings.claim: A generative storytelling reward model trained with reasoning distilled from teacher models reached 68% alignment with human creativity judgments.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Another data point that creative reward models land around 65-78% agreement with humans, so no picker will be near-perfect.

findings.claim: The EQ-Bench Creative Writing v3 benchmark says it controls length and position bias in its judge (truncation for Elo) and reports a judge-free 'slop' score from a list of over-used LLM phrases.
findings.source: https://eqbench.com/about.html and https://github.com/EQ-bench/creative-writing-bench (search snippet only, no paper)
findings.label: untested
findings.relevance: A slop-phrase count is a cheap, judge-free signal for the variety problem. I did not verify how it is implemented.

findings.claim: 333d does no selection. It returns the first of N333D=4 samples that passes guards G1/G2/G4/G5 (with at most 140 words), and the creative model sees only [system prompt + notebook facts, current user message], not the earlier chat.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: A learned picker would have real headroom, and the twin (whole chat) versus 333d (current message only) comparison mixes two differences. How often more than one candidate passes is unknown to me.

experiments.name: E1: small learned reward model picks among the 333d candidates that pass the guards
experiments.one_change: In install_creative333d, stop returning the first candidate that passes. Score all 4 candidates that pass the guards with Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2-1B, given the same system+facts+request messages, and return the highest-scoring one. Generation, guards, n=4, routing and the fallback line stay unchanged.
experiments.pass_mark: Fixed before running, on a new 40-request dev creative panel written without looking at the 333 panel, judged by the same blind judge. Validity precheck: at least 2 candidates pass the guards on at least 20 of the 40 requests; if not, report 'not testable' and stop. PASS only if all three hold: (a) useful >= 14/40 (333d baseline rerun on the same dev panel must also be reported; the gain must be >= +5); (b) invented person facts = 0; (c) the picked reply is the longest passing candidate on <= 60% of items with 2 or more passing candidates (chance is about 25-50%).
experiments.proves_wrong_if: Useful gains fewer than 3 over the 333d rerun on the same panel, or the reward model picks the longest candidate on more than 75% of multi-candidate items (it is a length picker, as in 2507.00769 Fig. 7 and 2310.03716), or invented person facts rise above 0.
experiments.cost: About $1 of rented 5090 time (40 x 4 generations with the 1B model plus 160 reward-model forward passes, minutes of GPU). New download: Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2-1B, about 2.5 GB, on the rented box only. Judge calls as in 333d.
experiments.brain_link: Dopaminergic valuation in the basal ganglia: several motor or verbal plans are prepared in parallel and a learned value signal gates which one is released, instead of releasing the first plan that clears inhibition. Later, the sleep phase could fine-tune this value model on replayed thumbs-up/down pairs (length-balanced).
experiments.novelty: Best-of-N with a reward model is standard (2507.01352, 2504.05228). Using a 1B reward model as the output gate of a notebook-grounded 1B assistant, behind hard no-invention guards, is not something I found published, but it is an engineering combination, not a new method.

experiments.name: E2: notebook-dependence picker (mutual information with the taught facts) instead of a groundedness count
experiments.one_change: Among the 333d candidates that pass the guards, pick the one with the largest summed PMI to the notebook facts: sum over reply tokens of [log p_MiniCPM(token | system+facts+request) - log p_MiniCPM(token | system+request)], computed by MiniCPM5-1B itself with thinking off. Everything else stays as in 333d. Requests with no context facts keep 'first that passes'.
experiments.pass_mark: Fixed before running, on the same kind of new dev panel, restricted to requests that have at least one taught fact available (target >= 20 such items). PASS only if all hold: (a) useful on those items beats the 333d rerun by >= 4; (b) invented person facts = 0; (c) 'fact echo' (the picked reply is <= 25 words and mostly restates a notebook fact without an idea, poem or plan, as marked by the blind judge's separate yes/no question) on <= 2 items; (d) the judge's blind yes/no question 'does the reply use something the user said earlier?' is yes on >= 60% of these items, versus the 333d rerun's own rate on the same items.
experiments.proves_wrong_if: Useful does not improve by at least 2, or the fact-echo count rises above 3 (the picker re-creates 333's 'grounded non-answer' failure), or fact use does not rise versus 333d.
experiments.cost: Under $1: 2 extra forward passes per candidate with the model already loaded (160 x 2 short passes). No downloads.
experiments.brain_link: Hippocampal contribution and source monitoring: a response counts as memory-based when the memory trace changes it, measured as the difference between recall with and without the cue, not by how much it looks like the memory. It directly rewards using taught facts. Because the notebook contains no invented facts, those facts get no PMI credit, and G2 stays as a hard veto.
experiments.novelty: The ingredients are published: MMI reranking (1510.03055) and the with/without-context contrast (2305.14739). Using that contrast against a personal exact-fact notebook as a picker score for creative replies is not something I found in my search. I would call it a plausible new combination (suggested), not a proven new method.

experiments.name: E3: audit the creative judge for length and position bias before trusting any picker result
experiments.one_change: Only the measurement changes, not Premonition. On the dev panel, add a length-controlled preference (logistic regression of the judge's A-vs-B verdict on the word-count difference, reported at zero difference, as in 2404.04475), run each pair in both orders, and add a gameability probe: for 20 dev replies, a padded copy with about 40% more generic words and no new content.
experiments.pass_mark: Fixed in advance: the judge is considered usable if it prefers the padded copy on <= 12/20 probes and the verdict flips with order on <= 6/40 pairs. The length-controlled preference must be reported next to the raw one for every future creative comparison.
experiments.proves_wrong_if: If the padded copy wins on >= 14/20 probes, or order flips on >= 10/40 pairs, the past comparisons (including 23/40 'preferred or tied') cannot be read at face value, and the judge prompt must change before E1 or E2 means anything.
experiments.cost: About $0.2 of judge calls plus no GPU. No downloads.
experiments.brain_link: Weak. This is instrument calibration, the equivalent of checking a thermometer, not a brain-like part.
experiments.novelty: Not novel. It applies 2404.04475 and 2410.02736 directly. It is ranked third because it doesn't change the assistant, but E1 needs it to be interpretable.

open_questions: How often do 2 or more of the 4 candidates in 333d pass the guards? If usually only one passes, no picker can help, and the bottleneck is generation or the guards (for example, G5's refusal regex may reject useful replies that contain 'without knowing').

Is the twin's 10/40 vs 333d's 8/40 due to the twin seeing the whole chat? The code shows the creative path sends only the current message plus retrieved facts. That confound should get its own single-change test, and with 40 items a difference of 2 is within noise.

The keyword router sent only 25 of the 40 creative requests to the creative path. A better picker only affects those 25, so a router change might be worth more than any picker. That is outside this angle.

Would a Skywork reward model trained mostly on general chat preferences value short gifts/toasts/plans the way the blind judge does? LitBench and Personalized RewardBench suggest 60-78% agreement at best; there is no evidence for this exact task.

Can the sleep phase collect honest preference pairs (the user's thumbs-up/down, or the user rephrasing after a bad reply) with enough volume and length balance to fine-tune a picker, without learning length or flattery?
How should variety be measured going forward: 'distinct replies per 1000' (surface-level) or NoveltyBench's functional-equivalence distinct_k? Surface counts may reward paraphrase noise.

verdict.angle: Skeptical check of the picking-and-judging report. I read the full PDFs, not just abstracts, for 2507.00769 (LitBench), 2507.01352 (Skywork-Reward-V2), 2604.07343 (Personalized RewardBench), 1510.03055 (Li et al. 2016), 2305.14739 (CAD), 2404.04475 (LC AlpacaEval) and 2410.02736 (CALM). I read scripts/claude_cre333d_agent.py, the sample_chat/_render code in claude_chat338_agent.py and context_facts in claude_cre333_agent.py. I searched for prior work on E2. I did not open any 333 panel or run outputs. Headline (shown): most numbers are right, but the report misreads one load-bearing source. In Personalized RewardBench, Skywork-1B was scored WITHOUT the user profile, and the paper shows that putting raw profile text into a reward model's input makes it worse. The report's case that E1 will reward correct use of taught facts therefore has no support. E2's novelty claim is also wrong: Nandwani et al. (EMNLP 2023) already proposed conditional PMI between a response and its grounding document, conditioned on the dialogue, as both a metric and a decoding method.

checks.claim: LitBench: reward models trained on 43.8k creative preference pairs reach 78% agreement vs 73% for Claude-3.7-Sonnet and 56-60% for small open judges; the report frames this as 'small learned reward models beat zero-shot judges'.
checks.note: Shown: the numbers match Sec. 5 and Table A.1 (43,827 pairs; 78%; Claude-3.7 0.731). But the 78% model is a Llama-8B Bradley-Terry model, not a small one. The '56-60%' judges are llama-3.1-8b (0.581) and qwen-2.5-7b (0.599), so 7-8B models, not 1B-class. Two things the report left out. First, the paper's own human study on freshly generated stories found annotators picked the RM-preferred story only 57% vs 41% of the time, and Claude-3.7 was 'at chance'. That matters directly for how far to trust Premonition's blind LLM judge. Second, the stories average about 550 words from Reddit WritingPrompts, far from 140-word gift or toast replies. The CoT figure (72%) is right, but it concerns GenRMs fine-tuned on distilled CoT. Using it to back 'run MiniCPM with enable_thinking=False' is untested extrapolation, and 333's thinking failure was in generation, not judging.

checks.claim: A Llama-3.2-1B BT reward model trained on creative pairs that were not length-filtered strongly preferred the longer story; length-balancing removed this.
checks.note: Shown (Sec. 5 'Validating Data Filtration', Fig. 7): the unfiltered 1.03M-pair set gave a 1B model that saturated at 70% and was 'length-biased, strongly preferring the longer of the two stories in most cases'. The second half is only suggested: the paper shows the length-balanced LitBench set trains a better model, but it reports no separate length-preference measurement for that model.

checks.claim: Skywork-Reward-V2 0.6B and Llama-3.2-1B: RM-Bench easy/normal/hard 90.3/78.0/54.8 and 91.3/79.9/57.8; the 0.6B is weak on RewardBench v2 Factuality (58.2) and Ties (34.0).
checks.note: Shown: Tables 4 and 5 match exactly. Omission: the 1B model that E1 actually proposes is also weak there (Factuality 60.9, Ties 43.1, Precise IF 45.6). The RM-Bench 'hard' split, where style favours the wrong answer, is only 57.8. So the 1B's resistance to style and length bias is modest. The 140-word cap, not the RM, is the main length control.

checks.claim: On Personalized RewardBench, Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2-1B scores 62.1/70.8/67.9, close to Claude-Sonnet-4-6 (67.3/70.7/73.6), so a 1B RM is about as good as frontier judges at telling which reply fits a particular user and is a plausible picker for replies that use taught facts.
checks.note: The numbers are shown (Table 2), but the interpretation is wrong. Sec. 4.1 says: 'Unless otherwise noted, we exclude the user profile u from the reward model input.' So these scores measure general-quality heuristics that happen to overlap with the rubric (App. B.2 says so explicitly), not reading the user. Sec. 4.3 and Fig. 2 show that 'naively injecting user profiles (w/ profile) degrades reward model performance'. Only a trained planner that turns the profile into rubric aspects recovers it. E1 does the naive injection: it puts system text plus notebook facts in the RM input. The paper predicts that is neutral-to-harmful, so E1's fact-use rationale is untested at best.

checks.claim: Li et al. 2016: likelihood ranking picks generic replies; MMI reranking with a tuned length weight gave more specific replies that humans preferred (alpha = 0.05).
checks.note: Shown overall (Tables 1-2 and 6; footnote 9: 'I don't know' and similar make up 32% of outputs). Small error: alpha = 0.05 is the significance level of the human test, not a model parameter. The weights are lambda and gamma, tuned by MERT. Caveats relevant to E2 (shown): human judges were told to prefer more specific outputs, which favours MMI by construction. The authors also warn that MMI-bidi reranking 'hinges on the initial generation of a highly diverse, informative N-best list', and 333d has only 4 samples. The MMI term there is p(message|reply) from a separately trained backward model, not a contrast against a notebook.

checks.claim: CAD (contrast with vs without context) improves faithfulness without training, e.g. +14.3% factuality for LLaMA in summarization, and helps most under knowledge conflict.
checks.note: Shown: +14.3% factKB is for LLaMA-30B on CNN-DM. Models tested were 2.7B-30B, and OPT 125M-1.3B in a size study that also benefited. It is a decoding-time logit adjustment on long source documents. Using it as a post-hoc score for short creative candidates is, as the report says, untested.

checks.claim: LC AlpacaEval: verbosity-prompt range for gpt4_1106_preview shrank from 22.9-64.3% to 41.9-51.6%; Arena Spearman correlation rose from 0.94 to 0.98.
checks.note: Shown (Sec. 4.1-4.2). Caveat: the length-controlled GLM is fit on 805 instructions across many models. A logistic regression on 40 A/B verdicts in E3 will have very wide intervals and must be reported with a CI. It is a sanity check, not a correction.

checks.claim: CALM: position bias gets worse with 3-4 options (robustness below 0.5 for most judges); sentiment robustness 0.65-0.80.
checks.note: Shown (Sec. 4, Fig. 6). Nuance: sentiment bias was tested by making the better answer on a fact dataset sound emotional (cheerful, sad, angry, fearful). The step to 'warm or flattering creative replies get rewarded' is suggested, not shown.

checks.claim: 333d does no selection: first of 4 samples passing G1/G2/G4/G5 (max 140 words); the creative model sees only system+facts plus the current message.
checks.note: Shown in scripts/claude_cre333d_agent.py:50-75. Also shown: sample_chat renders with enable_thinking=False (claude_chat338_agent.py:198). All 4 samples are generated in one call, so E1/E2 add no generation cost. Since samples are i.i.d., 'first that passes' is equivalent to a random pick among passing candidates, which makes the baseline a fair random-picker control. context_facts (claude_cre333_agent.py:53-62) always includes the user's own facts (up to 40). So E2's 'requests with no context facts keep first-that-passes' fallback will almost never fire, and PMI will be diluted by facts irrelevant to the request.

verdict.experiment_critique:
Strongest: E3, and it should run first because both E1 and E2 are graded by a judge whose reliability is unknown. LitBench's own human study found Claude-3.7 at chance on fresh generated stories. Weakest: E2 on novelty and mechanism, and E1 on its stated rationale.

E1 (Skywork-1B picker). It is one change and the precheck (at least 2 passing candidates on at least 20/40 items) is a good design. Problems:
(1) The fact-use rationale rests on a misread of 2604.07343 (see checks). Feeding the notebook facts into the RM is the 'w/ profile' condition that paper found degrading.
(2) The length check is weak. With 2 passing candidates chance is 50%, so '<= 60% longest' is within noise on about 20 items. Add a 'pick-the-longest' control scored on the same items to test whether the RM adds anything beyond length. That is extra measurement of the same generations, not a second change.
(3) There is a gray zone: pass needs +5, fail is below +3. Say in advance that +3 or +4 is 'inconclusive'.
(4) Paired 40-item power is low. +5 with, for example, 7 wins against 2 losses gives a sign test p of about 0.18. Pre-register a paired test, and measure judge test-retest noise by judging the baseline twice.
(5) 'Invented person facts = 0' depends on the judge. G2 only catches 'your <relation> <Name>', so a sycophancy-leaning RM could pick candidates that invent attributes of named people ('since Sarah loves hiking'). This needs a notebook-diff check, not only the judge.

E2 (PMI picker).
(1) The novelty claim is false. Nandwani et al. 2023 (arXiv 2305.12191, EMNLP; abstract-only) define conditional PMI between the response and the grounding document, conditioned on the dialogue, as a faithfulness metric and a decoding method. van der Poel et al. 2022 (2210.13210; abstract-only) use PMI decoding against hallucination. What remains new is only the application: a personal fact notebook and creative replies.
(2) Summed token PMI grows with length and with verbatim copying of fact tokens, so it is built to reward fact echo. The report expected this (pass mark c), but should use a length-normalized score or a length-matched check.
(3) The brain_link claim that 'invented facts get no PMI credit' is wrong (suggested failure). Tokens that invent attributes about a person named only in the facts are exactly the ones whose probability rises when the facts are present, so confabulation next to a taught name earns PMI credit.
(4) The without-facts prompt must be byte-identical minus the facts clause. The SYSTEM333D wording 'Facts the user has told you:' needs care.
(5) Pass mark (d) is not fixed: it is unclear whether it means at least 60% absolute, beating the baseline, or both. The falsifier 'fact use does not rise' has no margin. The gray zone between +2 and +4 is again undeclared.
(6) The subset of at least 20 fact-bearing items makes +4 noise-level.

E3. It changes only the measurement, which is fine. The padded-copy threshold (<= 12/20) is lenient. An unbiased judge should prefer the unpadded reply because padding adds nothing, so the expected rate is below 10/20 and 11-12 already hints at bias. Add a judge test-retest run and a small human check by Ben (for example, 20 items), because the pass marks for all three experiments depend on this judge.
verdict.missed:
(1) Direct prior work for E2: Nandwani et al. 2023 conditional-PMI faithfulness for document-grounded dialog (2305.12191) and van der Poel et al. 2022 PMI decoding (2210.13210). Both are abstract-only for me.
(2) Persona-dialogue candidate selection, the closest literature to 'pick the reply that uses the user's facts without contradicting them'. Dialogue NLI (Welleck et al., 1811.00671) and NLI-based persona consistency (1911.05889) use an NLI model to veto or rerank responses that contradict the persona. That is a learned alternative or backup to the regex G2 and fits the owner's preference for learned parts. SimOAP (2305.11130) oversamples and then post-evaluates for coherence and consistency. Post Persona Alignment (2506.11857) generates first and then grounds on retrieved persona facts. All are search-snippet only. They also weaken E1's novelty.
(3) BoN reward hacking and its fix: Regularized Best-of-N (2404.01054, snippet only).
(4) The headline implication of 2604.07343 Sec. 4.3: reward models need the profile turned into per-request rubric aspects by a planner. That lines up with WritingBench's query-specific rubrics and suggests a better E1 variant: have MiniCPM (thinking off) or the judge write 3-5 per-request criteria from the notebook facts, then score against them.
(5) Statistics: no noise floor or paired test for a 40-item panel, and no judge test-retest run. 8 vs 10 and similar gaps cannot be read without them.
(6) Bigger levers the report names but does not rank against the picker. The router sends only 25/40 creative requests to the creative path, and the creative path sees only the current message while the twin sees the whole chat. Each deserves its own single-change test, and either could matter more than any picker, because a picker only touches routed items with at least 2 passing candidates.
(7) Candidate-pool size: with N=4 and guards, Li et al.'s warning that reranking needs a diverse N-best list applies. The report never estimates how often 2 or more candidates pass. E1's precheck handles this, but it should be run first as a zero-cost count on a dev panel.

report.angle: Personalised creative help grounded in taught facts: (a) recognising a creative request in chat (learned intent classifier vs keywords), (b) choosing which stored facts to give the 1B model, (c) catching invented facts about real people (verification, constrained decoding, hidden-state probes), with brain-like learned parts that a sleep phase could train.
report.summary: Plain version for Ben: the research points to three places to fix, and they matter in this order. First, the front door. The keyword router is three pattern tests joined by AND (a cue word AND a request pattern AND NOT a recall pattern; scripts/claude_cre333b_agent.py:57-59), so any one miss drops the request. That is shown in the code and fits the 25/40 catch rate. Industry intent-detection work (2410.01627) shows that small trained classifiers and read-outs of an LLM's own internal state beat hand rules on real queries, though every system there still found out-of-scope rejection hard. Second, what the model reads. Memory benchmarks (LoCoMo 2402.17753, LaMP 2304.11406, LongMemEval 2410.10813) all find that a few relevant facts help more than a lot of loosely related ones. Our context_facts can pass up to 40 facts (every user fact plus one hop; scripts/claude_cre333_agent.py:53-62), which is a lot for a 1B model. Third, the fact-checker. Chain-of-Verification (2309.11495) and hallucinated-entity probes (2509.03531) show that checking claims one at a time, or reading a hallucination signal from the hidden states, cuts invented facts. Premonition has something those papers lacked: an exact notebook that says which facts about a person are true, so labels for training such a checker come free. PrefEval (2502.09597) also warns that telling a model to 'use the user's preferences' makes it invent preferences or refuse, which matches both the twin's 3 invented facts and the refusals in 333b/c. None of this is tested on MiniCPM5-1B. Every paper here used 7B+ models or benchmarks other than ours, so everything about Premonition itself is suggested or untested. My ranked plan: (1) swap the keyword router for a small classifier that reads MiniCPM's own hidden state (cheap, not novel, directly aimed at the 15 missed requests); (2) give the generator only the top 5 relevant facts; (3) later, a sleep-trained 'is this person-fact invented?' probe labelled by the notebook. I found no published version of (3).

findings.claim: The 333c/333d creative router is a conjunction of three regex tests (creative cue AND request pattern AND NOT recall pattern), so a request that misses any single pattern falls through to the ordinary reply.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Explains mechanically why recall is low (25/40). Any fix that ORs in a learned signal, or replaces the conjunction, targets the largest single loss in 333d.

findings.claim: 333d's context_facts passes every user fact, every fact whose subject or value is named in the request, and one hop out from those, capped at 40. There is no relevance ranking beyond literal string match.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: The 1B model may get many irrelevant facts. Whether it actually does on typical chats is untested; I did not look at panel chats.

findings.claim: On real deployed intent datasets, a contrastively fine-tuned small sentence encoder (SetFit + negative augmentation) averaged F1 0.658 vs 0.736 for the best LLM (Claude v3 Haiku), at about 1/56 of the latency. A hybrid that sends only uncertain queries (MC-dropout variance) to the LLM came within about 2% of the LLM at about 50% less latency. All models had poor out-of-scope recall.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Premonition's router is a two-class intent problem with a large out-of-scope side (look-alike non-requests). A tiny trained classifier is cheap and learned, but look-alike rejection is exactly where these systems are weakest.

findings.claim: Using an LLM's last-prompt-token hidden state from a decoder layer, compared by cosine similarity to stored training examples of the predicted intent, raised out-of-scope recall a lot for Mistral-7B (e.g. 0.205 to 0.950 on PowerPlay11; 0.376 to 0.782 on Curekart), at some cost to in-scope accuracy.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Suggests MiniCPM5-1B's own hidden states could drive the creative router with no new model download. Shown only for 7B; untested at 1B.

findings.claim: SetFit (contrastive fine-tuning of a sentence transformer, then a classification head) is competitive with full fine-tuning using as few as 8 labelled examples per class on some datasets, without prompts.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: An alternative router that needs a small (~100MB) encoder download. The owner could hand-label a few dozen examples. It is older than 2023 but is the standard baseline.

findings.claim: In LaMP, adding retrieved user-profile items improved all seven personalisation tasks. Even random profile items helped in most cases, but choosing relevant or recent items mattered, and no retriever won everywhere. Gains on the generation tasks were small (e.g. ROUGE-1 0.479 to 0.547 on email subjects, 0.159 to 0.177 on headlines).
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Supports selecting facts over dumping them. Also warns that personal context alone gives modest gains on open-ended generation, so the 1B model's base quality may cap usefulness.

findings.claim: Training the profile retriever with feedback from the downstream LLM (RL on a generation metric, or distilling which items helped the LLM) plus a per-input retriever selector gave statistically significant gains on 6 of 7 LaMP tasks.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: A brain-like option for the sleep phase: replay creative turns and teach the fact-selector which notebook facts made the reply better. Untested with a 1B generator and an exact triple store.

findings.claim: In very long conversations, RAG over short 'observations' (assertions about each speaker) beat raw logs by about 5% for gpt-3.5-turbo with the top 5 observations, and the gain faded as more observations were retrieved. Long-context models were easily misled into hallucinating (adversarial accuracy 2.1% for gpt-3.5-turbo-16k).
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Premonition's notebook triples are already observation-like. The finding that fewer, relevant items beat more supports a top-k cap on context_facts.

findings.claim: LongMemEval: expanding memory keys with extracted user facts raised recall@k by 9.4% and QA accuracy by 5.4%. Even with perfect recall, reading retrieved items well was hard, and Chain-of-Note plus a structured (JSON) format gave up to 10 points.
findings.source: arXiv:2410.10813 (Wu et al., ICLR 2025), Section 1 bullet list, Sections 5.3/5.5
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: The notebook is the fact-keyed index already. The reading finding suggests that how facts are formatted for the 1B model (plain sentences today) is another lever, but that is a separate change.

findings.claim: PrefEval: zero-shot preference following fell below 10% at 10 turns for most models. RAG and a simple 'Reminder' prompt were the best methods. Prompting methods made models hallucinate preferences, Claude 3 Sonnet gave many unhelpful refusals, and SFT on preference data beat RAG.
findings.source: arXiv:2502.09597 (Zhao et al., ICLR 2025), Sections 3.2-3.7, error analysis
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Mirrors Premonition's two failure modes: invented person facts (twin 3/40) and refusal-style non-answers (333b/c). It suggests the 'use the facts' instruction itself can push a model to invent facts.

findings.claim: PersonaMem: frontier models reached only about 50% accuracy at picking a response that fits a user's current, evolving profile from long histories.
findings.source: arXiv:2504.14225 (Jiang et al., COLM 2025), abstract and Section 1
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Personalised recommendation from chat history is hard even for large models, so a 1B model should be judged against realistic pass marks.

findings.claim: Chain-of-Verification (draft, plan verification questions, answer them independently, then revise) raised FActScore on long-form biographies from 55.9 to 71.4 (factor+revise) for Llama 65B, with few facts lost (16.6 to 12.3 per answer). Answering verification questions independently of the draft beat joint verification.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: For Premonition the verifier can be the exact notebook, not the LLM: extract each 'Person has attribute' claim from a draft and check it against stored triples. That is more general than the current regex G2 ('your <relation> <Name>'). Untested.

findings.claim: Linear probes on hidden states detected hallucinated entities token by token in long-form generation (AUC 0.90 vs 0.71 for semantic entropy on Llama-3.3-70B). They transferred across model families and enabled selective answering (abstain when risk is high). Models tested were 7B-70B, with labels from web-search annotation.
findings.source: arXiv:2509.03531 (Obeso, Arditi et al. 2025/2026), Fig 1, Sections 5.2, 5.4
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: A learned, brain-like 'this detail is made up' detector that could replace hand-written guards. Not shown at 1B. Premonition's notebook would supply the labels for person facts without web search.

findings.claim: Sparse-autoencoder directions in Gemma 2 (2B and 9B) encode whether the model recognises an entity, and steering them causally switches between refusing and hallucinating attributes.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Suggests even small models carry an internal 'do I know this person' signal that a probe could read. That signal concerns pretraining knowledge, not facts taught in chat, so transfer to notebook people is untested.

findings.claim: KCTS guides a frozen LM at decoding time with a knowledge-groundedness classifier (token-level via RIPA) plus tree search. It improved groundedness on knowledge-grounded dialogue and summarisation, with human raters scoring it more grounded while copying less knowledge verbatim than FUDGE.
findings.source: arXiv:2310.09044 (Choi et al., EMNLP 2023), Section 6, Table 4
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Constrained or guided decoding is an option for grounding, but MCTS per reply is too costly for a laptop-class assistant. Reranking a few samples with the same kind of classifier is a cheaper analogue (suggested).

findings.claim: HippoRAG models retrieval on hippocampal indexing theory: an entity graph with Personalized PageRank from the query's entities, with the LLM acting as neocortex.
findings.label: shown
findings.relevance: Brain-inspired precedent for selecting facts by spreading activation from the people named in a request. Premonition's one-hop expansion is a crude version of this.

findings.claim: Routing the 15 missed creative requests to the creative path would raise 333d's useful count.
findings.source: inference from 333d numbers in the task brief (8/40 useful; 25/40 routed)
findings.label: untested
findings.relevance: The creative path's per-request useful rate on routed items is not known to me (I did not open panel outputs), so the size of the gain from a better router is unknown. The twin's 10/40 suggests a ceiling near 10-12 for this 1B model.

experiments.name: Learned creative-intent router (hidden-state probe)
experiments.one_change: Replace is_creative333c with a logistic-regression probe on MiniCPM5-1B's mean-pooled final-layer hidden state (thinking off, the user turn only). Train it on a new, independently written set of about 150 creative requests and 150 look-alikes (recall questions like 'any idea what Maya likes?', teaching statements, factual questions, chit-chat), written without seeing the sealed 333 panel. Everything else in 333d stays the same.
experiments.pass_mark: Fixed now. Dev hold-out (20% of the new set): creative recall >= 0.90 and look-alike false positives <= 0.05. Sealed panel (run once): >= 34/40 creative requests routed AND <= 2/30 look-alikes routed AND end-to-end useful >= 11/40 with invented person facts = 0.
experiments.proves_wrong_if: On the sealed panel, routing <= 25/40 or false positives >= 4/30 (no better than keywords) means the 1B hidden state does not separate creative intent any better than rules. If routing reaches >= 34/40 but useful stays <= 8/40, routing was not the bottleneck and generation quality is.
experiments.cost: No new downloads (reuses MiniCPM5-1B). About 400 forward passes plus the 70-item panel and the 40-item end-to-end rerun; under 1 GPU-hour, about $1 on the 5090. Writing the labelled set takes a few hours of human or Claude time.
experiments.brain_link: A learned task-set selector (prefrontal context recognition) replaces hand-written rules. The sleep phase could retrain the probe on replayed turns labelled by whether the creative path helped.
experiments.novelty: Not novel as a method: hidden-state intent and out-of-scope detection is published for Mistral-7B (2410.01627), and SetFit is standard. Only applying it at 1B inside a sleep-retrained assistant is new here.

experiments.name: Top-5 relevant facts instead of up to 40
experiments.one_change: In 333d, change context_facts to return at most 5 facts. Facts about a person or thing named in the request come first; the rest are ranked by word overlap with the request (BM25 over the fact sentences). Ties go to the most recently taught fact. Router, prompt, guards and samples stay as in 333d.
experiments.pass_mark: Fixed now. Sealed panel: useful >= 11/40 AND invented person facts = 0 AND judge preferred-or-tied vs twin >= 23/40 (not worse than 333d). Also, on a dev set, the median number of facts passed must drop by at least half, or the change is void (nothing changed).
experiments.proves_wrong_if: Useful <= 8/40, or invented person facts > 0, means fact overload was not what limited the 1B model (or cutting context removed facts it needed).
experiments.cost: No new downloads. One 40-item end-to-end rerun plus a dev run; under 1 GPU-hour, about $1.
experiments.brain_link: Cue-driven hippocampal recall of a few relevant memories (pattern completion from the people and things named) instead of flooding working memory. Later, the ranking could be trained during sleep with LLM feedback, as in 2404.05970.
experiments.novelty: Not novel: top-k relevant retrieval is standard, and LoCoMo and LaMP show that selection matters. The test is whether it matters for a 1B model with an exact triple store.

experiments.name: Notebook-labelled invented-person-fact probe (research, after 09-30)
experiments.one_change: During sleep, generate creative drafts for dev prompts about people in the notebook. Label each draft's person-attribute spans automatically as supported or unsupported by the notebook triples. Train a linear probe on MiniCPM5-1B hidden states to flag unsupported spans. At wake, use it only to choose among 333d's 4 samples: take the passing sample with the lowest maximum probe risk instead of the first passing one.
experiments.pass_mark: Fixed now. Dev hold-out: span-level AUC >= 0.85 for unsupported person facts, and better than the regex G2 on the same drafts (probe recall at the same false-positive rate). Sealed panel: invented person facts = 0 AND useful >= 333d's 8/40 AND fallback count not higher than 333d's.
experiments.proves_wrong_if: Dev AUC < 0.75 (a 1B model's hidden states do not carry an 'I made this up about Maya' signal), or the probe catches no case that G2 misses on dev drafts.
experiments.cost: About 2-3 GPU-hours to generate and cache hidden states for about 2,000 drafts, about $2-3. Span extraction may need an offline judge pass (API dollars) or patterns. Fits one <= $4 job but not the remaining September budget alongside the other two.
experiments.brain_link: Reality monitoring and source memory: the prefrontal cortex checks whether a detail came from memory or imagination. Sleep replay supplies the training signal from the hippocampus-like exact notebook.
experiments.novelty: Hallucinated-entity probes exist (2509.03531) but use web-search labels on 7B-70B models. My search found no work that uses a personal exact memory as free labels to train such a probe in a sleep phase at 1B (novelty untested beyond that search).

open_questions: Of the 15 creative requests the router missed, how many would the 333d creative path have answered usefully? This decides how much experiment 1 can gain, and only a dev set built without the sealed panel should be used to estimate it.
How many facts does context_facts actually pass on typical dev chats? If it is usually under 5, experiment 2 is void.

Is the 1B generator itself the ceiling (twin 10/40 given the whole chat)? If so, routing and fact selection can recover only a few points, and a stronger or fine-tuned generator (PrefEval shows SFT beats RAG) is the real lever.

Does the SYSTEM333D instruction to 'use the facts below when they fit' push the model toward stretching facts (PrefEval's hallucinated-preference effect), and would a Chain-of-Note-style 'list the relevant facts first' help or hurt at 1B with thinking off?
Can a 1B model's hidden states separate creative requests from recall look-alikes ('any idea what Maya likes?')? Published results are for 7B+.
For the variety problem (45-59 distinct replies per 1000), does grounding on fewer facts make replies more alike? None of the papers read measured diversity together with personalisation.

verdict.angle: Skeptical check of the grounded-personal-creativity report. I read the cited code (scripts/claude_cre333_agent.py, claude_cre333b_agent.py, claude_cre333d_agent.py, claude_chat338_agent.py, fable_loop90_agent.py) and the full text of 8 cited arXiv PDFs (curl plus pypdf; no WebFetch). I also ran web searches for prior work, and I read three more arXiv abstracts; claims from those are marked abstract-only. I did not open the 333 panel or any run outputs.

checks.claim: The 333c/333d router is cue AND request AND NOT recall, so missing any one pattern drops the request (claude_cre333b_agent.py:57-59).
checks.note: Shown. is_creative333c returns _CUE333(low) and REQUEST333C.search(low) and not RECALL333C.search(low). claude_cre333d_agent.py:56 uses it unchanged. The report also says this 'fits the 25/40 catch rate'. That is suggested only: I did not check which pattern each missed item failed, because doing so would mean opening the panel.

checks.claim: context_facts passes every user fact, every fact whose subject or value is named in the request, and one hop out, capped at 40, with no ranking beyond string match (claude_cre333_agent.py:53-62).
checks.note: Shown. named |= {'user','me'}, then one hop over keep, then keep[:40]. The cut at 40 follows notebook order, not relevance. notebook_triples returns (subject, relation, value) with no timestamp, so experiment 2's 'most recently taught' tie-break needs extra code. The report missed one thing here: 333d already writes len(ctx) into loop.experience (claude_cre333d_agent.py:77-78). Open question 2 can therefore be answered from DEV rehearsal logs without GPU time and without touching the panel.

checks.claim: 2410.01627: SetFit+NegAug averaged F1 0.658 vs 0.736 for Claude v3 Haiku, at about 1/56 of the latency. The uncertainty-routed hybrid came within about 2% at about 50% less latency. Out-of-scope recall was poor for all models.
checks.note: Shown in the PDF. Table 1 has SNA avg 0.658 and Haiku 0.736, with latency 0.030 vs 1.697. The text says '56 times faster'. It also says the hybrid came within about 2% on in-distribution datasets (about 4% including OADP) at about 50% less latency. The SetFit encoder is MPNet (~110M). It is a multi-class intent setup with real customer queries, not a two-class creative-vs-look-alike task.

checks.claim: 2410.01627 Sec 4.2/Table 5: a last-prompt-token hidden state compared by cosine to training examples raised Mistral-7B out-of-scope recall (PowerPlay11 0.205 to 0.950; Curekart 0.376 to 0.782), 'at some cost to in-scope accuracy'.
checks.note: The numbers are right. 'Some cost' understates it: in-scope accuracy fell from 0.689 to 0.411 on PowerPlay11, 0.863 to 0.736 on Curekart and 0.842 to 0.767 on SOF Mattress. The method is also not a trained probe. Mistral-7B first predicts an in-scope label by prompting, then an out-of-scope check uses mean cosine similarity to the training sentences of that label. The method increases rejections, which trades away in-scope recall. Experiment 1 mainly needs the reverse (catch 15 more creative requests), so this paper supports the look-alike side of experiment 1, not the recall side. Experiment 1 also uses a different design: mean-pooled final layer plus logistic regression, at 1B. So the transfer is untested.

checks.claim: LaMP (2304.11406): profile items improved all seven tasks, random items often helped, choosing relevant or recent items mattered, and generation gains were small (0.479 to 0.547 email subjects; 0.159 to 0.177 headlines). The summary cites it as showing that 'a few relevant facts help more than a lot of loosely related ones'.
checks.note: The finding's numbers are right: Table 3, time-based split, LaMP-6T 0.479 to 0.547 and LaMP-4T 0.159 to 0.177. But they come from a fine-tuned FlanT5-base (250M) with k=1, which the report never mentions. The paper's Figure 2 says 'increasing the number of retrieved items leads to improved performance' for most datasets. That contradicts the summary's use of LaMP to back a top-5 cap. LaMP backs 'select relevant items', not 'fewer items'. In the zero-shot table (Table 4), LaMP-7 did not improve.

checks.claim: LoCoMo (2402.17753): RAG over observations beat raw logs by about 5% for gpt-3.5-turbo at top-5, the gain faded as more observations were retrieved, and long-context models hallucinated (2.1% adversarial accuracy for gpt-3.5-turbo-16k).
checks.note: Shown in Sec 6.1 and Table 3. Caveats the report leaves out: the task is question answering, not creative generation. The fade is small: overall F1 went from 41.4 at k=5 to 37.8 at k=50 for observations. For raw dialog retrieval, more items helped (31.7 at k=5 to 35.8 at k=25). The 2.1% is for full long context, not RAG. This is weak support for a hard cap of 5 on a 1B generator. The summary's 'all find' is overstated.

checks.claim: PrefEval (2502.09597): zero-shot preference following fell below 10% at 10 turns for most models. Reminder and RAG were best. Prompting methods led to hallucinated preferences, Claude 3 Sonnet gave unhelpful refusals, and SFT beat RAG.
checks.note: Shown in Sec 3.2-3.7, Fig 7 and Fig 10. SFT was on Mistral-7B and generalised to unseen topics. The report's mapping to 333d goes further than the paper. The hallucinated preferences came from prompting methods (Reminder, CoT, Self-Critic) when the model failed to recall a preference stated turns earlier. The paper says RAG reduced hallucination (for Mistral 8x7b). 333d puts retrieved facts in the system prompt, which is RAG-like. So 'the use-the-facts instruction pushes invention' is at best suggested for 333d. It fits the twin, which reads the whole chat, better.

checks.claim: 2509.03531: linear probes on hidden states detected hallucinated entities (AUC 0.90 vs 0.71 for semantic entropy on Llama-3.3-70B). They transfer across model families and enable selective answering. Models were 7B-70B, labelled by web search.
checks.note: 0.90 is the LoRA probe (0.9048). The linear probe got 0.8667 on LongFact for the 70B model and 0.8535 for Llama-3.1-8B, against semantic entropy at 0.714 and 0.719 (Table 1). The model range (Qwen2.5-7B to Llama-3.3-70B), the web-search labels, cross-model transfer (Fig 5) and selective answering (Sec 5.4) are confirmed. The report left out the stated limits: best LoRA probe about 70% recall at 10% false positives on long-form text; cutting hallucinations meaningfully in selective answering cost about 50% of correct answers; labelling pipeline 80.6% recall with 15.8% false positives. Training used about 8,000 long-form prompts per primary model, about 4 times experiment 3's 2,000 drafts. The linear probes here scored 0.85-0.87 at 8B-70B, so experiment 3's AUC ≥ 0.85 pass mark sits at that level, for a 1B model with less data.

checks.claim: CoVe (2309.11495): FActScore on biographies rose from 55.9 to 71.4 (factor+revise) for Llama 65B, with facts per answer from 16.6 to 12.3; factored verification beat joint.
checks.note: Shown in the Table 4 rows and the text ('28% (55.9 to 71.4)'). The base was a few-shot Llama 65B, not instruction-tuned.

checks.claim: 2411.14257: SAE directions in Gemma 2 2B and 9B encode entity recognition, and steering them switches between refusing and hallucinating.
checks.note: Shown in the abstract and the body (Gemma 2 2B and 9B, Figs 1 and 3). The report's caveat is correct: this is about knowledge from pretraining, not facts taught in chat.

verdict.experiment_critique:
Strongest: experiment 1 (learned router). It is one real change (the routing function), its dev hold-out pass mark is fixed in advance, and it cheaply targets a loss the code shows (a 3-way AND). Its flaws:
(a) The falsifier goes too far. A sealed-panel routing of ≤25/40 would show that a probe trained on Claude-written data does not generalise to the panel's wording. It would not show that 1B hidden states cannot separate creative intent. The dev hold-out answers the separability question, so say so.
(b) The cited evidence (2410.01627, Table 5) improves out-of-scope rejection at a large cost to in-scope recall (e.g. 0.689 to 0.411). That is the opposite of what the 15 missed requests need. Fix a threshold rule on dev (for example, the threshold that gives false positives ≤ 0.05) before the sealed run, and say so.
(c) Mean-pooled final-layer features are the least probe-friendly choice. Middle layers or the last token are usually better. Pick the layer on dev before sealing.
(d) Useful ≥ 11/40 is not a fair pass mark with 40 items. If the true rate stayed 8/40, sampling alone gives P(≥11/40) ≈ 0.16, before judge noise, and the twin already moved 9 to 10 between runs. Either raise the bar or use a paired comparison on the same items with a larger panel.
(e) The report's 'ceiling near 10-12' is untested: 333d could beat the twin, and the ordinary reply may already have made some of the 15 missed items useful. The ordinary-reply rate on missed creative requests can be measured on dev.

Weakest: experiment 2 (top-5 facts). It is not one change in effect. claude_cre333d_agent.py:61-62 builds the G2 'known' word set from the same fact sentences. Cutting to 5 facts shrinks 'known', so true names that fall outside the top 5 would trip G2 and cause more fallbacks. The prompt text changes too. The evidence base is also weak: LaMP's Figure 2 says more items help, and LoCoMo's fade is small and comes from QA. Its void clause (median facts must halve) is good. But the median can be checked now, for free, from the context_facts counts in DEV rehearsal logs. Do that before spending a run. If the median is under about 10, drop the experiment. The same 40-item noise problem applies to 11/40.

Experiment 3 (notebook-labelled probe) has a circularity problem. Labelling 'person-attribute spans' as supported or unsupported needs a claim extractor plus a notebook lookup. If that extractor works, it already is the verifier, run directly at wake (a CoVe-style check against the notebook), and needs no probe. The probe adds value only on claims the extractor misses, and the extractor's labels cannot teach it those. There are also problems with label truth. A fact missing from the notebook is not false, because the notebook is incomplete. And creative suggestions ('Maya might enjoy pottery') are not assertions. The 'better than G2' comparison is unequal: G2 only catches an invented Name after 'your <relation>', not invented attributes. The novelty claim is overstated (see missed work). Using an exact personal memory as free labels, trained during sleep, is a modest twist on known automatic-label pipelines, not a new method. The AUC ≥ 0.85 pass mark equals what linear probes reached at 8B-70B with about 4 times more data.

Across all three: every sealed run reuses the same 40+30 panel that 333, 333b, 333c and 333d already used, so repeated selection on it will overfit. Fix a fresh test panel, or limit the number of sealed runs allowed this month.
verdict.missed:
1) The biggest gap, shown in code: the 333d creative path gives MiniCPM only the system prompt, the notebook facts and the current turn. It never gives the chat history (claude_cre333d_agent.py:60-66; 338's chat path does include history, claude_chat338_agent.py:13-15). The twin it is compared with (10/40) read the whole chat. Anything said earlier that the reader did not store as a triple, plus pronouns and 'she'/'that trip' references, is invisible to 333d. So 'give the creative path the last N messages' (as 338 does) is a candidate single change that directly tests the 8-vs-10 gap. It is suggested and untested, and it may raise the risk of invented facts. The report attributes the gap to routing and fact overload without considering this.
2) Open question 2 already has data: loop.experience records context_facts per creative turn, so the DEV rehearsal logs can answer it for free.
3) Prior work missed for experiment 3, abstract-only: Lookback Lens (arXiv:2407.07071, EMNLP 2024). It detects contextual hallucination (unsupported by the given context, which is Premonition's case) with a linear classifier on attention ratios. It matched a hidden-state detector, transferred from a 7B to a 13B model, and was used for classifier-guided choice among sampled candidates. That is almost exactly experiment 3's wake-time use. Also HalluRAG (arXiv:2412.17056), which uses internal-state classifiers for closed-domain RAG hallucinations and reached up to 75% accuracy with limited generalisation. And Dialogue NLI (arXiv:1811.00671), which trains an NLI model on persona facts and reranks dialogue candidates for consistency with a persona: an old, cheap version of 'check the reply against stored person facts'. KCTS/RIPA (already cited) showed synthetic knowledge-shuffle labels. Web search also turned up 1B-3B grounding detectors (HaluCheck, snippet only). Together these make experiment 3's novelty claim suggested at best.
4) Missing statistics: nothing on how noisy a 40-item panel with an LLM judge is (about ±2-3 items). Nothing on panel reuse across 333 to 333d.
5) Experiment 1 lacks cheaper baselines to beat first: MiniCPM5-1B asked zero-shot 'is this a request for ideas or writing? yes/no' with thinking off (a learned model, one forward pass), and SetFit. Without them, a probe win cannot be credited to hidden states.
6) Nothing links the variety failure (45-59 distinct replies per 1000) to the proposed changes beyond one open question.
